//! Bounded, read-only evidence from the store's own commit clock.
use snapback4_core::{Engine, RuntimeError};
use std::collections::BTreeSet;

const SKIPPED_PREVIEW: usize = 32;
const TOLERANCE_MS: i64 = 5_000;
const RECENT_COMMITS: usize = 64;
const TABLE_BYTES: usize = 4096;
const TABLE_NAMES: usize = 8;
const REPORT_ERROR_BYTES: usize = 1024;
// Reserve one MiB for the outer clock/work envelope inside the host encoder.
// The reply retains `schedules` and its fired/held partition.
const REPORT_BYTE_BUDGET: usize = (crate::serve::JSON_RESPONSE_CEILING - (1 << 20)) / 2;

// @ref LLP 3000.007#20.12 — inspect a fixed recent commit window, never application row values.
pub fn ahead(engine: &Engine, now: i64) -> Result<Option<String>, RuntimeError> {
    // Reverse primary-key traversal: no full scan, sort, row payloads or retained
    // historical stamp set. octet_length(column) uses SQLite record metadata;
    // unlike a text length/cast/substr, it need not load oversized payloads.
    let mut lead = 0;
    let mut tables = BTreeSet::new();
    let mut omitted = false;
    engine.store().visit_recent_commit_clock(now.saturating_add(TOLERANCE_MS), TABLE_BYTES as i64, RECENT_COMMITS as i64, |record| {
        let at = record.at;
        if at <= now.saturating_add(TOLERANCE_MS) { return Ok(()); }
        lead = lead.max(at.saturating_sub(now));
        let length = record.length.ok_or_else(|| RuntimeError::Store("commit clock record is missing touched length".into()))?;
        if length > TABLE_BYTES as i64 { omitted = true; return Ok(()); }
        let bytes = record.touched.ok_or_else(|| RuntimeError::Store("commit clock record is missing touched bytes".into()))?;
        match serde_json::from_slice::<Vec<String>>(&bytes) {
            Ok(names) => for name in names {
                if tables.contains(&name) { continue; }
                if tables.len() < TABLE_NAMES && name.len() <= 128 { tables.insert(name); }
                else { omitted = true; }
            },
            Err(_) => omitted = true,
        }
        Ok(())
    })?;
    if lead == 0 { return Ok(None); }
    let mut names = tables.into_iter().collect::<Vec<_>>();
    if omitted { names.push("additional tables omitted".into()); }
    if names.is_empty() { names.push("no table names recorded".into()); }
    Ok(Some(format!(
        "N_CLOCK_STORE_AHEAD: recent commit stamps lead the current clock by up to {lead}ms (latest {RECENT_COMMITS} commits; tables: {}); use a fresh store per offset test ({}), or restart with the same --clock-offset (or dev --resume-clock) to continue",
        names.join(", "), crate::dev_clock::isolated_command())))
}

/// UTC calendar text for Unix milliseconds: schedule boundaries are UTC.
pub fn utc(ms: i64) -> String {
    let (days, rem) = (ms.div_euclid(86_400_000), ms.rem_euclid(86_400_000));
    // Civil-from-days (proleptic Gregorian), exact for the I53 range.
    let z = days + 719_468;
    let era = z.div_euclid(146_097);
    let doe = z - era * 146_097;
    let yoe = (doe - doe / 1_460 + doe / 36_524 - doe / 146_096) / 365;
    let doy = doe - (365 * yoe + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100);
    let mp = (5 * doy + 2) / 153;
    let day = doy - (153 * mp + 2) / 5 + 1;
    let month = if mp < 10 { mp + 3 } else { mp - 9 };
    let year = yoe + era * 400 + i64::from(month <= 2);
    format!("{year:04}-{month:02}-{day:02}T{:02}:{:02}:{:02}Z", rem / 3_600_000, rem % 3_600_000 / 60_000, rem % 60_000 / 1_000)
}

/// A positive duration in the units `clock advance` accepts, rounded up to a second.
pub fn span(ms: i64) -> String {
    let seconds = (ms.max(0) + 999) / 1_000;
    let (d, h, m, s) = (seconds / 86_400, seconds % 86_400 / 3_600, seconds % 3_600 / 60, seconds % 60);
    let parts: Vec<String> = [(d, "d"), (h, "h"), (m, "m"), (s, "s")].into_iter().filter(|(n, _)| *n > 0).map(|(n, unit)| format!("{n}{unit}")).collect();
    if parts.is_empty() { "0s".into() } else { parts.join("") }
}

/// Each schedule's saved boundary, in declaration order.
pub fn saved_boundaries(engine: &Engine) -> Vec<Option<i64>> {
    engine.schema().schedules.iter()
        .map(|schedule| {
            let shape = engine.store().schedule_shape(&schedule.name).ok().flatten();
            if shape.as_ref().is_some_and(|shape| *shape != snapback4_core::value::digest(schedule)) { return None; }
            engine.store().schedule_boundary(&schedule.name).ok().flatten()
        })
        .collect()
}

/// Preflight is bounded before the clock or worker leases change.
// @ref LLP 3000.007#20.12.1 — only explicit execution enumerates all crossed windows; coalesced reports keep a bounded preview.
pub fn crossed_boundaries(engine: &Engine, before: &[Option<i64>], now: i64, held: bool, each_boundary: bool) -> Result<Vec<(usize, i64)>, snapback4_core::Refusal> {
    let mut boundaries = Vec::new();
    let mut report_bytes = 0usize;
    for (index, schedule) in engine.schema().schedules.iter().enumerate() {
        // JSON may escape every error byte; count that bound per schedule.
        report_bytes = report_bytes.saturating_add(2048 + 6 * (REPORT_ERROR_BYTES + 3) + 8 * (schedule.name.len() + schedule.target.len()));
        if report_bytes > REPORT_BYTE_BUDGET { return Err(crate::dev_clock::input("schedule report exceeds its byte budget; reduce the declared schedules")); }
        if held { continue; }
        let Some(old) = before.get(index).copied().flatten() else { continue; };
        let end = schedule.boundary(now);
        if old >= end { continue; }
        let periods = schedule.periods_between(old, end);
        if each_boundary && periods > (10_000 - boundaries.len()) as i64 {
            return Err(crate::dev_clock::input("--each-boundary crosses more than 10000 schedule windows; use a smaller duration or omit --each-boundary to coalesce"));
        }
        report_bytes = report_bytes.saturating_add((if each_boundary { periods as usize } else { (periods as usize).min(SKIPPED_PREVIEW + 1) }).saturating_mul(1024 + 8 * schedule.target.len()));
        if report_bytes > REPORT_BYTE_BUDGET { return Err(crate::dev_clock::input("schedule window report exceeds its byte budget; use a smaller duration")); }
        if !each_boundary { continue; }
        let mut boundary = schedule.next(old);
        while boundary <= end {
            boundaries.push((index, boundary));
            boundary = schedule.next(boundary);
        }
    }
    boundaries.sort_by_key(|(index, at)| (*at, *index));
    Ok(boundaries)
}

// @ref LLP 3000.000.000.001#11-wave-22-loop-repairs-dx6 — no silent successful advance behind retained schedule markers.
pub fn refuse_held(engine: &Engine, before: &[Option<i64>], current_clock: i64, now: i64) -> Result<(), snapback4_core::Refusal> {
    for (schedule, saved) in engine.schema().schedules.iter().zip(before) {
        // Equality is the already processed current window, not a hold. The
        // authoritative requested clock defines the window, never wall time.
        if let Some(saved) = saved.filter(|saved| *saved > schedule.boundary(now)) {
            return Err(snapback4_core::Refusal::new("E_CLOCK_HELD", "clock", format!(
                "schedule {} already processed boundary {}; requested clock {} is in an earlier window; next unprocessed boundary is {}. Nothing advanced. Advance {} to reach the saved window or use a fresh staging deployment; allowHeld:true explicitly accepts this hold. Never rewind saved boundaries",
                schedule.name, utc(saved), utc(now), utc(schedule.next(saved)), format!("{}ms", saved.saturating_sub(current_clock)))).guide("clock"));
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn period(schedule: &snapback4_core::schema::Schedule) -> String {
    schedule.describe()
}

/// What each schedule did on one clock advance, and why one did not fire.
/// The core fires each schedule at most once per advance, for the latest
/// boundary, and holds it while its saved boundary is ahead of the clock.
// @ref LLP 3000#7-decisions-during-execution — missed boundaries fire once; this only explains them.
pub fn schedule_report(engine: &Engine, before: &[Option<i64>], fired: &[String], now: i64, current_clock: i64, held: bool, each_boundary: bool, port: Option<u16>) -> Vec<serde_json::Value> {
    let after = saved_boundaries(engine);
    // Read only bounded summaries: job args/cursors and full error payloads
    // are irrelevant to this report and must not be loaded then replicated.
    let runs = job_summaries(engine).unwrap_or_default();
    engine.schema().schedules.iter().enumerate().map(|(index, schedule)| {
        let (old, saved) = (before.get(index).copied().flatten(), after.get(index).copied().flatten());
        let current = schedule.boundary(now);
        let next = schedule.next(current);
        let mut entry = serde_json::json!({ "name": schedule.name, "target": schedule.target, "period": period(schedule), "fired": false, "firedWindows": [], "skippedBoundaries": [], "nextBoundary": utc(next) });
        if fired.contains(&schedule.name) {
            let end = saved.unwrap_or(current);
            entry["fired"] = true.into();
            let start = schedule.previous(end);
            let window = |boundary| serde_json::json!({"periodStart": schedule.previous(boundary), "periodEnd": boundary});
            let mut windows = Vec::new();
            if each_boundary {
                if let Some(old) = old {
                    let mut at = schedule.next(old);
                    while at <= end { windows.push(window(at)); at = schedule.next(at); }
                }
            } else { windows.push(window(end)); }
            if each_boundary {
                entry["reason"] = format!("fired {} windows: {}", windows.len(), windows.iter().map(|window| format!("{} to {}", utc(window["periodStart"].as_i64().unwrap()), utc(window["periodEnd"].as_i64().unwrap()))).collect::<Vec<_>>().join("; ")).into();
            }
            entry["firedWindows"] = windows.into();
            entry["periodStart"] = start.into();
            entry["periodEnd"] = end.into();
            if !each_boundary { entry["reason"] = format!("fired for the period {} to {}", utc(start), utc(end)).into(); }
            if let Some(run) = runs.get(&schedule.target) { entry["run"] = run.clone(); }
            // @ref LLP 3000.040#24-monthly-and-yearly-schedules — calendar periods count boundaries, not milliseconds.
            let skipped = if each_boundary { 0 } else { old.map(|old| schedule.periods_between(old, end) - 1).unwrap_or(0) };
            if skipped > 0 {
                entry["skippedPeriods"] = skipped.into();
                let mut windows = Vec::new();
                let mut at = schedule.next(old.unwrap());
                while at < end && windows.len() < SKIPPED_PREVIEW {
                    let mut item = window(at);
                    let mut args = serde_json::Map::new();
                    if let Some(program) = engine.program(&schedule.target) {
                        if program.args.contains_key("periodStart") { args.insert("periodStart".into(), schedule.previous(at).into()); }
                        if program.args.contains_key("periodEnd") { args.insert("periodEnd".into(), at.into()); }
                    }
                    item["command"] = format!("snapback4 run {} '{}'{}", schedule.target, serde_json::Value::Object(args), port.map(|port| format!(" --port {port}")).unwrap_or_default()).into();
                    windows.push(item); at = schedule.next(at);
                }
                entry["skippedBoundariesOmitted"] = (skipped - windows.len() as i64).into();
                entry["skippedBoundaries"] = windows.into();
                entry["reason"] = format!("fired once, for the latest period {} to {}; {skipped} earlier period{} this advance crossed (from {}) did not run: missed boundaries fire once. Run {} with periodStart/periodEnd for an earlier period",
                    utc(start), utc(end), if skipped == 1 { "" } else { "s" }, utc(old.unwrap_or(end)), schedule.target).into();
            }
        } else if held {
            entry["holdCode"] = "disabled".into();
            entry["reason"] = "schedules are held (dev --hold-schedules or --replay); a restart without the flag resumes at the next boundary".into();
        } else if let Some(saved) = saved.filter(|saved| old.is_some() && *saved > current) {
            let due = schedule.next(saved);
            entry["holdCode"] = "saved-boundary".into();
            entry["savedBoundary"] = saved.into();
            entry["heldUntil"] = utc(saved).into();
            entry["nextBoundary"] = utc(due).into();
            entry["reason"] = format!("held by the store: boundary {} was already processed and this clock {} is in an earlier window (restarting resets the process offset, not the saved boundary). One fire per boundary. Advance {} more to reach the saved window, or use a fresh staging deployment/store for an independent test; keep the same --clock-offset when continuing a test across serve restarts",
                utc(saved), utc(now), span(saved.saturating_sub(current_clock))).into();
        } else if old != saved {
            entry["holdCode"] = "initialized".into();
            entry["reason"] = format!("{} started at boundary {}: a schedule fires at the boundary after the first one it sees, next {} ({} from now)",
                if old.is_none() { "this schedule" } else { "this changed schedule" }, utc(saved.unwrap_or(current)), utc(next), span(next - now)).into();
        } else {
            entry["holdCode"] = "not-due".into();
            entry["reason"] = format!("next boundary {} ({} from now; schedule times are UTC)", utc(next), span(next - now)).into();
        }
        entry
    }).collect()
}

// @ref LLP 3000.000.000.001#10-wave-20-loop-repairs-dx5 — every declared schedule has one reported outcome.
pub fn outcomes(schedules: &[serde_json::Value]) -> (Vec<serde_json::Value>, Vec<serde_json::Value>) {
    schedules.iter().cloned().partition(|schedule| schedule["fired"] == true)
}

/// The report never loads full error/argument payloads from retained jobs.
fn job_summaries(engine: &Engine) -> Result<std::collections::BTreeMap<String, serde_json::Value>, RuntimeError> {
    let mut summaries = std::collections::BTreeMap::new();
    for summary in engine.store().job_summaries(REPORT_ERROR_BYTES)? {
        let name = summary.name;
        if summaries.contains_key(&name) { continue; }
        let mut error = summary.error;
        let truncated = summary.error_truncated;
        if let Some(text) = &mut error && truncated {
            let mut end = REPORT_ERROR_BYTES.min(text.len());
            while !text.is_char_boundary(end) { end -= 1; }
            text.truncate(end); text.push('…');
        }
        summaries.insert(name, serde_json::json!({ "id":summary.id, "state":summary.state,
            "rowsWritten":summary.rows_written, "error":error, "errorTruncated":truncated }));
    }
    Ok(summaries)
}

/// Startup lines for schedules the store holds: their saved boundary leads the clock.
pub fn held_schedules(engine: &Engine, now: i64) -> Vec<String> {
    engine.schema().schedules.iter().zip(saved_boundaries(engine)).filter_map(|(schedule, saved)| {
        let saved = saved.filter(|saved| *saved > schedule.boundary(now))?;
        let due = schedule.next(saved);
        Some(format!("clock     schedule {} is held until {} ({} from now): its saved boundary {} is ahead of this clock; `clock advance {}` or restart with dev --resume-clock",
            schedule.name, utc(due), span(due - now), utc(saved), format!("{}ms", due - now)))
    }).collect()
}

/// The dev clock offset that continues a store's own time: its newest
/// recent commit stamp (or saved schedule boundary) less wall time, never negative.
pub fn resume_offset(store: &snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore, wall: i64) -> Result<i64, RuntimeError> {
    let commit = store.recent_commit_max_at(RECENT_COMMITS as i64)?;
    let boundary = store.latest_schedule_boundary()?;
    let latest = commit.into_iter().chain(boundary).max().unwrap_or(wall);
    // Whole seconds, rounded up, so restarting twice does not drift backwards.
    Ok((latest.saturating_sub(wall).max(0) + 999) / 1_000 * 1_000)
}

pub fn has_data(engine: &Engine) -> bool {
    engine.store().inspection_has_data().unwrap_or(false)
}

pub fn offset_line(offset: i64, running: bool) -> String {
    format!("clock     offset from wall time: {offset:+}ms{}", if running { " (lasts until restart)" } else { " (no running dev; inspecting against wall time)" })
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    fn engine() -> Engine {
        let bound = snapback4_lang::compile(&[("schema.q".into(), "table alpha:\n  at: time\n  public\ntable beta:\n  at: time\n  public\n".into())]);
        assert!(bound.diagnostics.is_empty(), "{:?}", bound.diagnostics);
        Engine::new_at(snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore::memory().unwrap(), bound.schema,
            bound.programs.into_iter().map(|p| p.program), 100_000).unwrap()
    }
    fn seed(engine: &mut Engine, table: &str, commit_at: i64, row_at: i64) {
        engine.seed_at([(table.into(), snapback4_core::value::object([
            ("id", snapback4_core::Value::Id(snapback4_core::ids::mint(row_at, &mut snapback4_core::ids::Mint::default()).unwrap())),
            ("at", snapback4_core::Value::Int(row_at)),
        ]))], commit_at).unwrap();
    }
    #[test]
    fn clock_report_bounds_one_large_job_error_repeated_across_many_schedules() {
        let mut source = "table rows:\n  n: int\n  public 'fixture'\njob tick():\n  for row in rows:\n    update rows[row.id] {n:1}\n".to_owned();
        for n in 0..500 { source.push_str(&format!("schedule s{n} every 1m: tick\n")); }
        let bound = snapback4_lang::compile(&[("schema.q".into(), source)]);
        assert!(bound.diagnostics.is_empty(), "{:?}", bound.diagnostics);
        let mut engine = Engine::new_at(snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore::memory().unwrap(), bound.schema, bound.programs.into_iter().map(|p|p.program), 0).unwrap();
        engine.fire_schedules(0).unwrap();
        let before = saved_boundaries(&engine);
        assert_eq!(crossed_boundaries(&engine, &before, 60_000, false, true).unwrap().len(), 500);
        let fired = engine.fire_schedules(60_000).unwrap();
        let message = "🧪\n\\".repeat(30_000);
        (match engine.store() { snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore::Sqlite(inner) => inner }).test_support_conn().execute("UPDATE _jobs SET error = ?1 WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM _jobs ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1)", [&message]).unwrap();
        let report = schedule_report(&engine, &before, &fired, 60_000, 60_000, false, false, None);
        assert_eq!(report.len(), 500);
        assert!(report.iter().all(|s| s["run"]["errorTruncated"] == true));
        assert!(report.iter().all(|s| s["run"]["error"].as_str().unwrap().len() <= REPORT_ERROR_BYTES + 3));
        assert!(serde_json::to_vec(&report).unwrap().len() < 2 << 20);
    }
    #[test]
    fn clock_report_refuses_before_the_host_encoder_limit() {
        let mut source = "table rows:\n  n: int\n  public 'fixture'\njob tick():\n  for row in rows:\n    update rows[row.id] {n:1}\n".to_owned();
        for n in 0..3000 { source.push_str(&format!("schedule s{n} every 1m: tick\n")); }
        let bound = snapback4_lang::compile(&[("schema.q".into(), source)]);
        assert!(bound.diagnostics.is_empty(), "{:?}", bound.diagnostics);
        let mut engine = Engine::new_at(snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore::memory().unwrap(), bound.schema, bound.programs.into_iter().map(|p|p.program), 0).unwrap();
        engine.fire_schedules(0).unwrap();
        let before = saved_boundaries(&engine);
        let refusal = crossed_boundaries(&engine, &before, 60_000, false, true).unwrap_err();
        assert_eq!(refusal.code, "E_CLOCK_INPUT");
        assert!(refusal.message.contains("byte budget"));
        assert_eq!(before, saved_boundaries(&engine));
        assert!(REPORT_BYTE_BUDGET < crate::serve::JSON_RESPONSE_CEILING);
    }
    #[test]
    fn utc_text_and_spans_match_the_calendar() {
        assert_eq!(utc(0), "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        assert_eq!(utc(951_782_400_000), "2000-02-29T00:00:00Z");
        assert_eq!(utc(-1), "1969-12-31T23:59:59Z");
        assert_eq!(utc(1_791_468_000_000), "2026-10-08T14:00:00Z");
        assert_eq!(span(12_633_000), "3h30m33s");
        assert_eq!(span(86_400_001), "1d1s");
        assert_eq!(span(0), "0s");
    }
    #[test]
    fn resume_offset_follows_the_newest_commit_and_is_never_negative() {
        let mut engine = engine();
        assert_eq!(resume_offset(engine.store(), 100_000).unwrap(), 0);
        seed(&mut engine, "alpha", 3_700_500, 1);
        assert_eq!(resume_offset(engine.store(), 100_000).unwrap(), 3_601_000);
        assert_eq!(resume_offset(engine.store(), 9_000_000).unwrap(), 0);
    }
    #[test]
    fn commit_tolerance_and_largest_lead_ignore_future_application_values() {
        let mut engine = engine();
        seed(&mut engine, "alpha", 100_000, 1_000_000);
        assert!(ahead(&engine, 100_000).unwrap().is_none());
        seed(&mut engine, "alpha", 105_000, 2_000_000);
        seed(&mut engine, "beta", 107_000, 3_000_000);
        let note = ahead(&engine, 100_000).unwrap().unwrap();
        assert!(note.contains("up to 7000ms (latest 64 commits; tables: beta)"), "{note}");
        let note = ahead(&engine, 99_999).unwrap().unwrap();
        assert!(note.contains("up to 7001ms (latest 64 commits; tables: alpha, beta)"), "{note}");
        assert!(ahead(&engine, 102_000).unwrap().is_none());
    }
    #[test]
    fn recent_window_does_not_claim_older_commits_or_read_row_payloads() {
        let mut engine = engine();
        seed(&mut engine, "alpha", 200_000, 200_000);
        for n in 0..RECENT_COMMITS { seed(&mut engine, "beta", 100_000, 300_000 + n as i64); }
        // Deliberately unreadable images: metadata inspection must not deserialize them.
        (match engine.store() { snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore::Sqlite(inner) => inner }).test_support_conn().execute("UPDATE r SET data = 'not json'", []).unwrap();
        assert!(ahead(&engine, 100_000).unwrap().is_none());
        (match engine.store() { snapback4_core::store_port::AnyStore::Sqlite(inner) => inner }).test_support_conn().execute("UPDATE _commits SET at = 200000, touched = ?1 WHERE seq = (SELECT MAX(seq) FROM _commits)", ["x".repeat(TABLE_BYTES + 1)]).unwrap();
        let note = ahead(&engine, 100_000).unwrap().unwrap();
        assert!(note.contains("100000ms") && note.contains("additional tables omitted"), "{note}");
    }
}

  assert.equal(next.fired[0].name,"expiryHourly","the next unprocessed window fires once");
  assert.equal((await host.drain()).held[0].holdCode,"not-due");
} finally {await host.stop();}

# LLP 3000.000.000.002: Declarative release backfills

**Type:** RFC
**Status:** Review
**Systems:** Snapback 4 language, storage, release adoption, staging clock, proof kit
**Author:** Codex for Charlie Cheever (MIG)
**Date:** 2026-10-19
**Revised:** 2026-10-21 (EVOL, wave-21 adoption, previews, bridges and migration expressiveness); 2026-10-19
**Related:** [Release activation](./3000.000.000-retained-storage-and-hot-release.rfc.md), [Staging](./3000.000.000.001-staging-with-real-users.rfc.md)

## 1. Commission

Implementer: MIG, 2026-10-19. Wave 17's fifty changes require constant,
conditional, derived, enum, string-split and point-lookup transformations.
Declare these in Quarry, with no public migration mutation, job or JavaScript.
REL5 owns release selection/restoration and old-client compatibility; SEC3 owns
security checks. No new version, publication or push authority is implied.

## 2. Language

A top-level declaration describes one table's historical input fields and its
simultaneous output patch:

```quarry
backfill bookings vehicleClass(weight: int, length: int):
  { vehicleClass: 'commercial' if weight > 3500 else 'van' if length >= 500 else 'car' }
```

Here length is stored in centimetres. Arguments are typed historical fields;
they remain in the declaration after the candidate drops those fields. The
compiler binds arguments against their explicit types, not today's table.
The runtime validates them against each interpreted historical row. Output
names belong to candidate authoritative columns and may equal input names:
read-old/write-new. Outputs of multiple declarations on a table must be
disjoint. Names are unique per table. Durable store history keeps one
normalized definition per table/name, including gaps; changing it refuses with a
bridge/new-name repair. A new name denotes a new transformation.

The expression body is an object patch. It uses Quarry's existing arithmetic,
comparisons, null handling, conditional expressions, immutable helper expansion,
and bounded deterministic scalar builtins. Supported text additions are
`before(text, delimiter)`, `after`, `beforeLast`, `afterLast`, `startsWith`,
and `allDigits`. Splits remove the first/last exact delimiter; absent delimiter
means whole text before, empty text after. An empty split delimiter refuses.
Digits means nonempty ASCII digits. Text is Unicode, comparisons and splits
are locale independent. Existing `lower`, `trim`, `slice`, `count`, `sha256`,
`first`, `last`, `at`, `min`, `max`, exact `divide`, calendar/civil transforms
and concatenation retain their normal checked semantics. No randomness,
viewer, clock, minted ids, writes, mutation helpers or loops are admitted.
Identity `id` is never an output. Only scalar outputs are admitted, including new references. Assets, lists,
engine-owned/captured/maintained and lifetime outputs refuse, including fields
owned by a historical source lifetime even when the candidate removes that rule.
Restored narrowed rows retain their individual output ownership, captures and
reference types. Columns added by later predecessor schemas contribute their
own types/defaults only when absent from that archived definition. Overwriting an
existing reference/asset is refused: derive a new reference column so the
existing dormant reference-lifetime ledger owns retirement/restoration.

Point reads use the ordinary `members[principal = owner] ! else NOT_FOUND`
spelling. They require a unique point. A missing asserted point refuses;
ordinary nullable point reads and `exists` retain their explicit semantics.
Historical existence predicates may traverse a metered source range, needed
for wave-17 cross-tower references; they return no row collection. A meter
cut is a refusal, never false absence or an incomplete historical value.
Before evaluating any patch, each unique lookup index validates the historical
population's cardinality with bounded privileged duplicate samples. A different
simultaneous patch making candidate keys unique cannot choose an arbitrary old
match. All reads run as the trusted activation system principal, bypassing application
read rules, against the assembled historical snapshot. Dormant namespaces
remain unnameable. Candidate read indexes are built over that source snapshot
only when their component fields exist there. No JavaScript or app migration
operation receives this authority. All declarations are self-contained: they
cannot read another declaration's outputs in the same activation.

## 3. Adoption and reversibility

The existing activation writer transaction owns this sequence:

1. Assemble retained source rows/cells and their source definitions using the
   existing restoration intent. This includes narrowed rows eligible to return:
   restore their full historical images before evaluation, deferring only the
   backfill output columns' candidate-type checks. Retained reference invalidation,
   source lifetime and audience checks still apply before restoration. Retire
   source-expired lifetimes before any backfill; a transform cannot extend an
   expiry or opening boundary.
2. When leaving a declaration, restore its predecessor-visible output fields
   from saved **output preimages**, separately from its argument inputs. Save
   interpreted old values, including literal defaults/nulls, and absence.
   Added output columns use ordinary dormant retention instead. A different
   current value from both recorded output and preimage refuses with a conflict;
   untouched same-column enum renames restore their exact original value.
   Membership is per row lifetime, with normalized declaration definitions kept
   beside evidence. Removing a whole table suspends its membership rather than
   feeding transformed values back as inputs. Re-entering that declaration reads
   its original overwritten inputs and preserves its current result; selecting
   original source instead reverses it even when the immediately previous schema
   lacked the table/declaration. Ordinary active deletion clears membership.
3. Enter declarations absent from the immediately active schema. Unchanged
   carry-forward and reopening run none for ordinary active rows: candidate-native
   writes are not historical rows. Newly restored narrowed rows receive carried
   declarations too, including a declaration introduced while they were dormant. On re-entry, restored cells/rows are eligible along with
   older active rows. A native v2 row whose absent historical inputs have a
   complete valid restored output image keeps that image. Older v1 rows lacking
   outputs are filled. Declarations must accompany skipped-release source;
   no unseen intermediate transformation is implicitly inferred.
4. Evaluate every entering patch against one assembled source snapshot, with
   ordinary per-row job meters and a paged source walk. Stage output/evidence
   in SQLite temp storage before applying any patch. Recompute the patch on
   re-entry, so changed lookup values count as changed dependencies even when
   declared arguments are unchanged. Compare both saved argument values and
   computed outputs. If unchanged, preserve edited added-column cells. If
   changed, recompute only when current outputs equal the saved result or the
   reversed preimage; otherwise refuse the conflict. Never overwrite a manual
   output edit because another input happened to change. A fully reversed
   same-column output edited during absence also refuses re-entry when its
   current interpreted value equals neither preimage nor saved result, even
   with unchanged arguments. Sparse defaults count by interpreted value.
5. Apply patches and evidence together. Run ordinary narrowing/reference
   closure, projection, complete type/asset validation, indexes, uniqueness,
   caps and maintained-data rebuilds. Transformed dependencies force rebuilds
   even when their declarations did not change. Publish programs, generation
   and release in the same commit. Any error rolls everything back.

Evidence is keyed by table number, row lifetime and the SHA-256 digest of the
normalized declaration/typed IR (no diagnostic locations or whitespace).
It records declared input values, each overwritten output preimage and computed
output. Ordinary authoritative deletion/expiry deletes that row's evidence in
its transaction; id reuse cannot inherit it. Row moves to dormant storage
preserve lifetime. Backfill definitions enter schema/activation identity;
changed rows also set activation population, forcing a fresh generation and
device reacquisition. Public/device schema projections omit all backfill
metadata; devices never execute migrations. A successful evidence installation
sets `snapback4-release-store-6`, transactionally. Unaware binaries refuse that
format even when an old source is selected. Failed installation retains the
previous format. Legacy stores without backfills remain unchanged. Prune previews
backfill preimages separately, with counts, bytes and bounded ids. Explicit
prune deletes their values and keeps only per-lifetime reversal-unavailable
identities. Leaving an overwritten column then refuses with a pruned-preimage
reason: select a bridge retaining present meaning or restore a backup. Active
row deletion clears these identities too. Pruning added-column evidence does
not prevent rollback when no old-visible field needs a preimage.

Dropping a declaration has explicit semantic meaning: leave it by restoring
preimages or refusing conflicts. Keep declarations in every later source
whose view should retain their meaning. Refusals include exact affected counts
and up to five bounded privileged samples. Missing inputs/lookups, output/type
errors, arithmetic/meter errors and uniqueness/cap conflicts refuse atomically;
a widened/optional non-unique bridge plus an authorized repair mutation is the
repair path. A post-backfill-edit conflict requires keeping the current/bridge
source, deciding a truthful old representation, then repairing it before
selecting old source. No automatic fallback turns a new enum value into an old
meaning. Native v2 rows with no preimage retain the parent's existing law:
forward selection may make incompatible present values dormant; rollback
requires representability and refuses with its existing reason. This amendment
does not change REL5's rollback or restoration selection policy.

`deploy --check` uses the existing private disk snapshot, deploy direction and
restoration intent; rollback previews use rollback direction. Later live writes
can change its plan. `backfills` in both cold/hot JSON receipts and exact preview
text reports `table name transformed N rows` or `table name reversed on N rows`.
These are transformed row visits, separate from the parent's disjoint dormant
rows/cells/index entries. They are not additive counts of distinct rows across
different transformations, and do not claim a frozen production population.

Consumed historical references must retain valid parent-lifetime evidence even
when the input column is dropped. Expired predecessor/restored images are retired
before any transform, including ordinary expiry without read-through. Pruning
keeps membership-only tombstones solely for surviving lifetimes; such a tombstone
refuses re-entry requiring lost values rather than treating the row as fresh.

Re-entry retains an adoption-cohort identity with each active row receipt.
All declarations first applied in one activation, including continuously carried
declarations on tables that were never removed, read one reconstructed source
snapshot, including point/range indexes; this overlays that cohort's complete
input evidence and output preimages (including original absence) on current
images. Distinct original cohorts are evaluated separately against their
respective historical overlays, so a declaration introduced later can read an
earlier declaration's already-transformed values. Computed and retained/native output values must fit candidate scalar types and
text minimum/format constraints before narrowing; invalid generated outputs
refuse the entire adoption with affected-row samples. Patches remain staged until
all cohorts succeed, and current row images are restored before applying them.
New declarations use the current assembled predecessor snapshot. Inactive
cohorts restore their own still-omitted input interpretations, independently of
new declarations in that activation, and catch up changed authored inputs. Declared historical arguments consume retained
cells and source definitions even when the candidate omits those columns;
retained parent-lifetime bindings still apply. A native-image exception requires a birth marker for this exact declaration,
a matching fingerprint of the original non-output inputs, and valid, complete outputs;
a new declaration never skips valid old inputs merely because an older
transformation left a retained output. Receipt reference inputs use private namespaced bindings in the existing
dormant parent-lifetime ledger, independently of the live input column. A
retargeted/dropped input cannot substitute its current binding for the saved
reference. Every unchanged saved argument consumed during active or inactive
re-entry validates its private lifetime binding before program evaluation.
Bindings use each restored narrowed row's actual archived reference type
(rather than the table-wide predecessor), even when an
argument is declared as generic `id`. Existing private bindings survive
re-entry with unchanged saved inputs even after the visible column becomes
generic `id`; schema type erasure cannot recapture the same parent id. Reconstruction validates any consumed saved binding before restoring
its value. Original absence is recorded separately from the predecessor's interpreted
value. A physically missing field consumes its source default when present,
otherwise null; receipts retain that interpretation explicitly, preventing
later defaults from changing argument or lookup/index evaluation. Expired sources retire when entering or leaving the
last declaration, including restored table images.

When transformed rows become dormant, candidate output reference types supply
parent bindings even when the predecessor had no such column. Existing invalid
bindings are preserved. If a restored row becomes dormant again, only its
explicitly backfilled authoritative cells update the retained image; original
source definition, other cells and authority provenance stay intact. Forward
selection after rollback reconstructs absent added outputs for that same
declaration before evaluating its arguments, rather than feeding it its own
retained result.

Input omission is stored independently from interpreted null/default values,
both for the current physical lifetime and for each receipt. Ordinary writes
compare interpreted old/new inputs; meaningful edits end omission provenance,
while unrelated writes and default materialization do not. Receipts reconstruct
their original interpretation of omitted fields across later default changes.

Rows inserted while a declaration is active receive a private native-birth
marker keyed by its normalized definition and a hash of their input image;
no original input values are kept in that marker. The same declaration preserves
complete native images with unchanged inputs, including absent optional inputs,
constant transforms and whole-table restoration. Changed native inputs, invalid
present inputs, lost native output images or conflicting other-transform history
refuse with a bridge reason. An inactive overlapping receipt is compatible only
when every overlapping current output equals its recorded preimage; an active
or pruned conflicting history still refuses. Same-column output values belong
to the candidate type, rather than the historical input type, for native rows.
A new declaration name does not inherit another
name's birth marker. Prune retains only native fingerprints for surviving
lifetimes, alongside current omission flags; receipt absence flags are forgotten
with historical values. Delete/reset remove every marker for the ended lifetime.

Source retirement uses the ordinary engine expiry/reference-action closure
under the complete assembled predecessor schema, before any patch runs or
removed table is archived. Only surviving post-action rows enter dormant storage. Restored source
indexes and cap occupancy are rebuilt first; writing-reference groups must fit
the source reservation's live bound. Cascade and set-null effects participate
in this same transaction; restrict or retained-child blockers refuse the entire
adoption. Retired source population forces a new generation so clients cannot
keep children removed by a cascade. Authoritative set-null updates corresponding archived cells/narrowed images
to null before clearing old column bindings, while receipt input bindings remain
independent. An expired
narrowed source is exposed only inside this uncommitted lifecycle phase and
cannot reach a backfill evaluation alive.

Development reset still empties every lifetime's data/history/native/omission
markers, then reconstructs code-derived declaration/input registries from its
retained schema before reseeding; the new identity's rows receive new birth
markers. No release HTTP reset door is added.

Evidence decode is preflighted against
the existing job heap ceiling. Text preview lists private preimages separately
from dormant application rows/cells/index entries.

### Per-column transformed views

A receipt records a `retained_outputs` set independently of its declaration's
active flag. When leaving a declaration, candidate-visible transformed outputs
reverse to their preimages. Outputs absent from the candidate remain transformed
in dormant storage; their set membership survives until reversal or re-entry.
Even an inactive declaration reverses those suspended fields when a later plain
schema exposes them. Whole-table suspension keeps the transformed view intact.

Re-entry preserves the saved preimage for each still-transformed output. A
fully reversed output instead captures its actual assembled source value,
including restored dormant cells and interpreted predecessor defaults, before
applying the patch. Input history and rollback preimages are separate: an input
may retain its original omitted/null interpretation while the latest rollback
view has a literal default. Ordinary writes do not erase omission provenance
when they edit a transformed output from that same original cohort.

An inverse restoring genuine absence records a transaction-local source mask.
Later evaluation cannot fill that absence from the suspended result or a default
belonging to the output schema. The mask is dropped on every exit. Earlier
recorded cohorts' staged patches are replayed into later recorded source views;
fresh declarations still share the untouched predecessor snapshot and cannot
read each other's newly staged outputs. Every decode remains heap-admitted.

Reference arguments copy any matching ordinary cell-lifetime bindings before
restoration consumes that ledger, including transformed reference cells absent
from an archived whole-row definition. Unchanged saved inputs retain existing
private bindings; inferred current bindings cannot overwrite their invalidation.
The stable format is `snapback4-release-store-6`, with schema capability
`release-backfills-v3`. Published 0.4.33's store format 3 upgrades on first use.
Unpublished experimental formats 4/5 and the older capabilities cannot silently read
this evidence layout. Package versions are not changed in this workstream.

## 4. Staging clock

Wave-20 reporting amendment: LLP 3000.000.000.001 §10 changes the proof
advance return to `{now, fired, held}` and explains persisted boundary holds;
operator authority and clock execution semantics below are unchanged.

Only a store durably classified staging by deploy --staging may serve with
--clock-offset. Missing/unknown classification is production. This setting
is process-local, with the same signed-duration parser and monotone elapsed
clock as dev. No serve-time mechanism can reclassify an existing production store. Restart drops the offset unless explicitly
provided again; persisted timed-disclosure floors never retreat below their captured value.

Staging exposes the existing /dev/clock/status and /dev/clock/advance only
with any full service session: these are trusted operator credentials, as for
system jobs. Production refuses even with a service token, and an explicit
production serve offset refuses with E_CLOCK_DEV_ONLY before listener startup. Account, guest, read-only and unauthenticated
requests refuse. Recheck classification and session under the engine writer
before advancing. All fixture, reset, persona and dev-job doors remain closed.
Use the same advance implementation, schedule drain and ambiguous-reply law
as dev. CLI clock advance --release DIR mints its local service authority.
startServe accepts clockOffset and exposes now()/advance() through that
operator authority; it never changes store classification. Each helper control
mints a current staging-time operator session rather than caching a credential
across arbitrary time jumps. Ordinary user sessions retain normal expiry.

Hot release activation samples `shared.now()` under its engine writer, including
the persisted disclosure floor, and passes that one time through the core's
explicit `adopt_release_at`. A live preview probes the existing filesystem owner lock independently of
HTTP bind/address hints and acquires a stopped-store lock before taking its
SQLite snapshot, retaining that lock through inspection. A rollback preview
reuses its caller's existing ownership rather than probing its own lock as a
live host.
A live preview samples time through the same-owner,
store-bound existing private status protocol; no session is minted or clock
changed. A missing existing-store ownership sidecar refuses rather than assuming a
stopped host without exclusion; ordinary rollback preview can reestablish and
reuse its canonical ownership. A revision mismatch with the private database snapshot refuses as a
racing activation. Store contents and the clock are point-in-time samples, not
a freeze of later live writes. A stopped store's cold activation/preview uses
wall time, with the existing persisted disclosure floor applied by activation.
Positive and negative staging offsets are both covered by hot/preview tests.

## 5. Evidence

Tests cover all fifty historical shapes, no-op/restart, v1 writes during
rollback, same-column enum reversal, edited-output refusal, missing lookup,
invalid output, uniqueness failure, deletion/id reuse, generation reset and
hot/cold/preview equivalence. The guide's persistent production recipe uses
real users and operator role setup, tests tightened privacy and declares its
invariant, rolls back and forward with business assertions. Its exact fences
run against the fresh packed tarball. Reproduce five copied bakeoff lanes,
record actual line/time deltas. Run required crate/client/differential/Linux,
Mac Studio clock tests, refs, budget and root checks.

## 6. Reviews

Round 1: [Muse](./reviews/3000.000.000.002-mig-r1.muse.txt) and
[fresh Codex](./reviews/3000.000.000.002-mig-r1.codex.txt) returned NOT READY.
This revision specifies historical eligibility, exact preimages, lookup changes,
phase order, immutable declaration identities, reference/asset restrictions,
format/generation fences and bounded bridge repairs. It retains strict conflict
refusal rather than Muse's suggested silent edited-row preservation: preserving
a different same-column value under old semantics could change business meaning.
The author explicitly permits rollback refusal with a reason.

The [fifty-shape executable inventory](../snapback4/crates/snapback4-core/tests/backfills/wave17.json)
tracks every line of `~/sb4-loop/wave17/changes.txt`. Exact source solutions are

## 7. DORM reverse views and migration primitives

The proposed [DORM amendment, LLP 3000.000.000 §19](./3000.000.000-retained-storage-and-hot-release.rfc.md#19-dormant-visibility-and-migration-dorm)
extends the existing backfill machinery with standalone typed `down`
declarations and identical-type column rename declarations. It supersedes
§3's native-row policy only where an explicit reverse projection provides
the old view. Ordinary saved forward preimages, source retirement, immutable
typed-IR definitions, meters, cohort conflict checks and atomic release
publication remain binding. Native values with no old representation remain
dormant. Existing backfills re-enter on forward selection and process rows
written under the older source; no implicit cross-table fanout is invented.

Down evidence shares per-lifetime retention/prune custody, with explicit
projected-cell ownership across repeated rollback/forward cycles. It cannot
overwrite a conflicting old-source edit. Legacy null cells may have been
materialized by an earlier rollback, so they do not establish a native birth
or a genuine non-null predecessor value. A standalone down declaration may
explicitly fill those nulls from the newer source; missing asserted reads
still refuse and no fallback is inferred. The parent amendment defines the
precedence, scalar/lifetime boundaries, source identity and inspection law.

The new runtime writes `snapback4-release-store-7` and declares
`release-backfills-v4` when its migration metadata is present. It reads prior
committed format 6 and upgrades transactionally; an older runtime refuses
format 7 rather than interpreting new evidence. Source rollback remains
supported on the newer runtime. This work does not change package versions.
Readiness and final qualification are recorded with DORM's reviews/report;
the earlier MIG READY pair applies only to the previous semantic revision.


## 8. Wave-21 release evolution

Implementer: Codex for Charlie Cheever (EVOL), 2026-10-21; target 0.4.37.
This amendment supersedes the insert-only input policy in §3. Ordinary
writes while the exact declaration is active refresh existing native input
fingerprints. They do not create native birth evidence for migrated rows.
Active forward receipts refresh only actually edited, currently authored
non-output inputs and their reference lifetime bindings. Overwritten historical
inputs, original output preimages, omission interpretations on unrelated
writes, inactive receipts and immutable definitions retain their custody.
An older-release edit does not receive this refresh. At re-entry a changed
input is compatible when deterministic recomputation over the assembled source
produces the exact stored output; an incompatible edit without accepted native evidence still refuses.
Valid native outputs written under the owning declaration remain authored
values, even when they differ from the historical transform. Refresh replaces
the fingerprint, rather than accumulating old accepted images.

Rename destination conflicts consult only physically present or retained cells.
An absent optional destination is absent; interpreting it as null or a default
cannot manufacture a conflict. Explicit present null is still a real cell.

SEC6 owns rule-changing deploy review items, write intent, projection privacy
and client session validation; EVOL does not change those contracts.


A table declares `table observations renamed from behaviors:`. It moves the
same numeric table identity and row/reference lifetimes, never copies rows or
merges independent histories. Both names cannot appear together in a selected
schema. The durable name relation permits old-source rollback and older-source
writes to return under the newer name. Existing independent destination storage
refuses atomically. Indexes, retained type definitions, asset homes and migration
receipts follow that identity; literal values and operation names do not change.
Store format 8 and the release-table-renames-v1 capability fence the new metadata.

`rollback --check --bridge DIR` now writes the selected target's complete source,
loosening only differing compatible value domains to their union with current
source and retaining new authoritative tables with their current rules. It lists
changes and direct target read/write operations on affected tables. It never changes immutable
source or activates automatically. The generated bridge is a new deployable
release, subject to ordinary compilation/adoption. Incompatible nominal types,
new business logic, current guards absent from v1, and old UI assumptions about
null require explicit review; diagnostics and the app-specific checklist remain
visible. A retained new table does not claim a frozen v1 operation exposes it.
No reverse projection fabricates an asset, reference, list element or missing
table. Scalar `down` remains the answer for a truthful scalar substitution;
loosened bridges cover nullable files/images, empty image lists and optional
money without invented placeholders.

Preview causes are recorded by the actual narrowed-population closure: a column
and incompatible value category, or a typed reference to a hidden parent. Counts
may overlap across causes and are schema populations before read rules. New-table
rows have a separate cause. Foresight consults declared reverse writers rather
than calling their old output absent. SEC6 owns review-item resurfacing.

Asset columns (`file`, image/video and asset lists) use `renamed from` as an
identity move, rather than computed scalar forward/down substitutions. The
active and retained physical cells and the ledger's one home move together;
selecting old source changes the public name back, preserving current values.
Both aliases cannot be active together; a conflicting physical/retained cell
refuses atomically. Reference/captured/engine field renames remain excluded.
Older runtimes refuse store format 8; device projections omit migration metadata.

Cross-table historical existence and unique point reads are first-class
backfill inputs under §2's assembled-source, metered system authority. A guide
example must include the source index and explicit row input rather than an
application reconciliation loop. Outputs remain disjoint scalar patches and
all declarations observe the same pre-patch snapshot.

`fileText(file)` is a migration-only deterministic input, accepted in backfill
and down expressions, including through pure helpers. It reads the immutable
retained file named by the ledger, as UTF-8. It never reads an application path
or URL, unverified bytes, arbitrary ids, or a device's filesystem. The runtime
requires an internal migration context and charges the job heap and step meter
before reading at most the ledger byte length plus one. Absent bytes, released
assets, length disagreement, invalid UTF-8 or meter exhaustion refuse the whole
adoption. Preview reads the same original immutable asset root while writing
only its private database snapshot. The feature creates no user-callable
migration operation and does not make arbitrary file contents readable to users.
`nonemptyLines(text)` counts trimmed nonempty lines, including repeated entries
separately; CRLF and whitespace-only lines have their ordinary text meaning.
It is a pure scalar transform; an empty textual list counts zero. A generated
scalar is reversible through the existing output-preimage/evidence custody;
fileText never mutates the bytes or their home. Ordinary new-order byte validation
is outside this release-migration primitive; it receives no invented enforcement
claim from a historical backfill.


### EVOL review clarifications

“Exact declaration” means its normalized typed-IR digest, not a release number.
A declaration can be carried in later source. “Currently authored” means a
column present in that selected schema whose interpreted value actually changes
in an application write; hidden inputs and overwritten migration arguments are
excluded. “Older-release edit” means a write while this exact declaration is
absent. Replacing accepted non-output inputs intentionally forgets their previous
live values: this is live data, not a history of every application write. It
never forgets an overwritten output's reversal preimage. For migrated rows the
parent's dependency/output comparison still applies, with exact recomputation
agreement added for both transformed and fully reversed cells. Native rows with
matching refreshed non-output fingerprints and valid complete outputs preserve
their authored images. A fingerprint mismatch needs full recomputation agreement
or refuses; it never authorizes overwriting a different authored image.

A helper inherits the migration context transitively when expanded. Calling a
helper containing fileText outside a backfill/down refuses during compilation;
raw IR also refuses at execution without the unforgeable internal context/root.
Failure in a forward migration, down, or exact preview aborts that entire
transaction. Preview has the identical job precharge and file validation.
File-read failures never print raw bytes. Output scalars are deliberately
authored data under their destination rules; an author copying file text into
a readable text column must choose its audience explicitly, as for any backfill.
No automatic output or diagnostic exposes the input bytes. Asserted missing
points refuse the whole operation. Nullable points preserve §2's ordinary
nullable semantics only through the author's explicit expression; no missing
point becomes an invented preimage. The database snapshot pins ledger and point
reads; asset bytes are immutable under their ledger id, read at exact length.

Rename conflicts compare a destination cell not owned by the moving alias in
the same surviving row lifetime. They do not compare the source cell against
itself or consult dead row lifetimes. Table moves keep their numeric identity;
independent destination identities cannot be merged. Asset renames never revive
a released asset. A selected schema still validates every moved asset against
the ledger/type. Reference, captured and engine-field renames are diagnosed
before activation, rather than silently losing their bindings.

The bridge's compatible joins are: identical underlying types with optionality
union; integer bounds with the lower minimum and higher maximum; matching-kind assets
with the higher byte limit (file MIME and image-once policy unchanged);
same-format text with the lower minimum and higher maximum; enum member
union; lists with recursively compatible element types, lower minimum and higher
maximum. Other nominal/type conversions are not guessed; they remain target
domains, are listed for explicit typed repair, and receive no promise of complete
visibility. Existing compiler diagnostics and the checklist expose operations
needing adaptation; readers AND writers on affected tables are listed. The
bridge never executes a scalar asset projection: it changes only the selected
schema's value domain over the same retained actual cells. Old nullable UI
assumptions remain an application compatibility check, not a claimed guarantee.
It keeps one alias for a renamed table, selecting the target's spelling; the
other name remains only in the durable identity relation. That spelling routes
old reads/writes to the same numeric row lifetime. It never adds both aliases as
independent tables. Existing target rule/intent text remains byte-identical;
new tables retain current rule text. Ordinary deploy preview reports current
safeguards the target lacks. SEC6 owns rule-review resurfacing; EVOL adds no
blocking review gate or invented safety guarantee.

A cause is either `(table,column,incompatible-value-category,target-type)` or
`(table,column,hidden-parent-table)`. Activation first hides incompatible rows,
then iterates typed reference edges until no additional dependent hides. Only rows physically in the current active `r` namespace immediately before
activation contribute to these preview counts; already dormant rows do not.
Neither source nor target application read rules filter this denominator. A row may have more
than one cause, so cause counts are explicitly non-additive; total hidden rows
are distinct. New-table rows are counted separately. Static foresight compares
possible future domains and declared reverse writers; exact preview runs the
actual activation against current data. Both are privileged local operator
outputs, never per-user query results or public HTTP metadata. Private preview
writes are removed, never published to the live database or generation.


The native and migrated re-entry algorithms are distinct. Native acceptance is
available only when the row has NO forward evidence receipt for the declaration
and has its native marker. A migrated row NEVER gains that marker from an edit.
For each migrated row, every re-entry evaluates the patch again against its
reconstructed inputs and current point dependencies, regardless of whether saved
inputs compare equal. Refreshing its non-output inputs/bindings changes that
input basis, not its `after` computed-result baseline or output preimages. If
fresh computation differs from saved `after`, a stored output equal to the old
computed result, reversed preimage, or fresh computation permits writing the
fresh computation, never retaining a stale value; a different manual output
conflicts. Successful adoption records the fresh computation as `after`. If inputs and computation are unchanged,
the parent's explicit edited-added-cell preservation rule applies. Thus a live
retarget P1 → P2 with O=f(P1) never skips computation at re-entry: it either
recomputes to f(P2) or refuses a conflicting edited O. Backfill is an activation
transform, not steady-state maintained-data enforcement. A native image whose
current input fingerprint matches its accepted native marker instead preserves
its complete valid authored outputs; a mismatching native image needs exact full
recomputation agreement or refuses. These branches cannot substitute for each
other.

Bridge operation listing covers direct lowered Quarry read/write table sites,
including expanded pure helpers. It is a conservative table-level diagnostic,
not a complete dependency proof: indirect rule dependencies, actions, external
workers and frozen UI assumptions require the checklist's manual workflow audit.
The lack of a complete-visibility promise for incompatible type conversions says
nothing about the separate operation-listing diagnostic. No listing grants
authority to deploy or replaces ordinary compiler/adoption validation.

For avoidance of doubt, “active” in visibility accounting is a storage state,
not a viewer's source-rule result. With 1,000 physical active rows and 400 denied
to some viewer, all 1,000 are in the privileged preview denominator. With 600
physical active rows and 400 already dormant, only 600 are in that denominator.
If the target hides 100 of those 600, `hiddenRows` is 100. No source/target rule
predicate is executed to convert that into a per-user number. This preserves the
parent DORM contract and cannot leak to an app caller: the tool is local operator
inspection only.


In the migrated branch, `deps_same` means BOTH input values and fresh computed
patch equal their saved counterparts. If inputs change but the patch equals
saved `after`, `deps_same` is false: the fresh patch is written when the current
output equals saved `after`, its preimage, or that same fresh patch; any other
manual value refuses. Matching more than one allowed baseline has no precedence
ambiguity: each allows writing the same single fresh patch. Only `deps_same`
plus a still-transformed, present output invokes the parent's explicit preservation
of edited added cells. Every successful staged receipt records fresh inputs and
fresh `after`, retaining the correct predecessor preimages.

If both a native marker and a forward receipt for the same digest are present,
the receipt takes precedence: evaluate the migrated algorithm and its exact
baseline/preimage custody. The marker cannot skip that computation. This overlap
is not produced by ordinary writes (which never create a native marker on a
migrated row), but precedence is explicit for retained/legacy state. Pruned
membership is checked first and cannot become native acceptance. Down receipts
have distinct down digests and do not establish native-forward status.

“Affected” for bridge listing includes domain-loosened tables, retained new
authoritative tables, and identities whose table/asset-column spelling moves.
Use the target spelling for a renamed identity, with its current spelling noted
as provenance; never list the aliases as two independent tables. Emit direct
lowered Quarry readers/writers on those tables. The separate manual audit still
covers indirect rule/action/worker/UI dependencies.

## Summary

Eighteen Clique calibrations sit on a plateau: holistic 88–92, with
`data_modeling`, `queries_and_live` and `scale_and_limits` at the bottom in
every window (LLP 3000.012 §2.1). Every `data_modeling` note charges the cost
of learning Quarry's execution model, and most charge a read model the
application maintains or a capacity number the author chose. 0.3.0 moved
three derived forms into the engine and the calibration did not move
(`data_modeling` 87, `queries_and_live` 90).

The remaining cost is the surface itself. A query names the index it scans
(`by byAuthorTime`), hand-merges lanes (`[h] for h in range(hour(now) - 24,
hour(now) + 1)`) and states bounds the engine could choose (`first 10001`,
`size authors 2000, edges 20000`, `cap 60000`). Each derived form has its own
grammar and its own limits. A typed reference can silently select a parent
scan instead of the row it names. The builder has to learn the engine's cost
model to state what the product means.

Charlie authorized significant rework (2026-09-23: "if you need to try making
*significant* architectural reworks in order to make the data modeling,
queries, and scalability be excellent and elegant, you can experiment with
that. I'm not attached to things being the way they are now."). This RFC
decides that rework:

1. **Reads state intent; a planner chooses how.** `posts where .authorId =
   owner last 20 by .at after c`. The compiler chooses or synthesizes every
   index. Queries, rules, sync lines, caps and expiry never name one.
   Time-window rankings become bucketed lane merges without authored lanes.
2. **One derived-data declaration, `view`.** The engine picks the strategy:
   filters, projections and unions are planned at read time; aggregates are
   maintained in the writing transaction; Following is materialized per
   reader.
3. **Following without caps.** Delivery to followers becomes engine-owned
   background work, so a post acknowledges in constant time. Reads hide
   unfollowed authors immediately. Promotion, pull routes, broadcast lanes and
   every author-visible cap leave the design.
4. **Work without bounds.** Aggregates over reads stream instead of
   materializing pages. Job loops chunk themselves. `emit … once` replaces
   marker tables.
5. **A paved client.** One app object owns sign-in, restore and the durable
   outbox. One command gives a web export an offline shell.

The engine, rules, partitions, prediction, metering and IR stay. The rework
is a planner and desugarer in front of the binder, three engine additions
(merge-lane projection, background delivery, streaming aggregates), and the
client.

## 1. Evidence

**Observed** (calibration #18, `benchmarks/runs/2026-09-23-snapback4-clique-astra-0.3.0/`):

| Category | Score | The scorer's charge |
|---|---:|---|
| data_modeling | 87 | "restrictive program shapes and unfamiliar compiler vocabulary"; "subtle reference-driven index selection" |
| queries_and_live | 90 | "Global needed a separate event table, and queries required explicit bounds and carefully shaped merges" |
| background_work | 89 | "atomic per-recipient digest computation potentially parking at job bounds" |
| client_integration | 92 | "Cold web launch required an authored app-shell service worker; native lifecycle evidence stops at builds" |
| scale_and_limits | 90 | "builder diagnostics, not the full independent probe matrix; finite work ceilings remain relevant" |

The builder's 542-line backend carries 25 `by` lines, 12 `sync` lines, eight
`cap` lines and a timeline `size` clause, none of them product rules except
`cap 50 by conversationId`. It also carries three application tables that
hold derived or bookkeeping state (`events`, `dmPairs`, `digestMarkers`) and
a hand-shaped 25-lane Trending merge. Its diary: "The difficult part was
understanding when a typed reference selects a parent index rather than an
id lookup." Its essay: the author must learn "a bounded prefix, a held query,
a maintained value, a source horizon".

An independent assessment (a separate Claude session, relayed by the author
on 2026-09-23) reached the same place from the design: the language shows
the engine's cost model instead of hiding it; the derived forms are separate
features that did not compose by default; the timeline carries sizing numbers
in application code; the next gains come from simplifying the core language.
What it said would change its answer: one general derived view that the
engine maintains; a planner, with bounds inferred and defaulted; data
modeling at parity with SQL on this brief; evidence beyond one app and one
builder.

**Interpretation.** The strongest categories (media 98, authorization 97)
are the ones where a declaration on a table does the whole job. The weakest
are the ones where the author must also say *how*. The fix is to let the
author say only *what*, everywhere, and to move the *how* into a planner and
the engine.

## 2. Reads state intent

### 2.1 Predicate reads

```quarry
query userPosts(owner: principal, c: cursor ?):
  return posts where .authorId = owner last 20 by .at after c postCard
query thread(postId: posts, c: cursor ?):
  return replies where .postId = postId first 20 by .at after c
query trending():
  return posts where .at > now - 1d and .at <= now last 10 by .likeCount, .at postCard
```

A read is `T where P`, optionally followed by `matching q`, a page clause
(`first N` ascending or `last N` descending), `by K1, K2, …` and `after c`,
then an optional shape. Order keys are columns (`.at`), including
engine-maintained columns. `id` is always the final tiebreak in the same
direction. Without `by`, the order is `id`. Ids are time-ordered, so
`last N` is newest first. Without a page clause the read is a domain: the
whole matching set, bounded as today by a schema cap or the meter, and
chunked in a job (§5.2).

Supervisor ruling (2026-09-24): in a table order, every key after `id` is
redundant because `id` is unique within that table. The planner truncates the
order at `id`: `by .id, .at` plans exactly as `by .id`, using the existing id
index without a duplicate component or new index. View orders are not
truncated: ids may coincide across branches, and branch identity breaks any
remaining tie after the projected order keys.

The planner splits `P` into top-level conjuncts:

| Conjunct | Plan |
|---|---|
| `.c = e`, with `e` independent of the row | an equality pin on `c` |
| `.c < e`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on the first order key | a seek |
| a range on a `time` column other than the first order key, with finite lower and upper bounds (`now - D` and `now`, `D` constant) | bucketed lanes over every intersecting bucket: `hour` for a window ≤ 48h, `day` for ≤ 92d; the exact endpoints stay as filters, so the page is exact. With only one bound the window is not finite, and the read is an ordinary residual scan with a note that adds the missing bound |
| `.c in e`, with `e` a bounded list or one column of a read (`members where .principal = viewer`)`.conversationId` | one lane per value |
| anything else | a residual filter, evaluated after the read rule, under the meter |

The 0.4.1 Workroom ruling (2026-09-24) makes ordering comparisons on nullable
scanned-row columns inside `where` false on null. A seek on such a column
excludes nulls: an upper-only seek has an exclusive null lower bound.
Equality and inequality with null remain total. Nullable arguments/locals and
comparisons outside predicates keep their presence checks.
Seek extraction, including an explicitly ordered page, requires a present,
infallible endpoint before the predicate runs. Required bindings and literals
qualify; arithmetic qualifies only with a proof against overflow. Division and
optional bindings guarded within the predicate stay residual, preserving
short-circuit evaluation and narrowing.

Required enums of at most eight variants plan `!=` a literal or stable bound
value as membership in the remaining variants. Nullable enums and larger
enums remain residual; nullable inequality retains null rows. Fallible
exclusion expressions remain under their original predicate guards.
Value lanes require a proof that every lane prefix decides the source read
rule, including any nullable fallback lane. Otherwise membership and enum
inequality stay residual on an ordinary scan, preserving its continuation
through visible rows without claiming completeness for a non-uniform rule.
Certificates render residual membership as membership, not its lowered
boolean initializer; fully extracted predicates have no residual clause.

The optional-filter ruling (2026-09-24) recognizes `(a = null or C)` in
either disjunct order (also accepting `==` in this idiom). `a` must be an
optional argument or a local derived only from arguments. `C` must be a
pinnable equality, bounded membership, or range with a safe endpoint that
uses `a` and no other optional input. Up to three distinct inputs receive
presence alternatives; additional conjuncts remain residual and are named
by `N_OPTIONAL_FILTER_LIMIT`. Each alternative uses ordinary index planning
and admission. The runtime selects it before the scan, removing an absent
input's conjunct and narrowing a present input. Streaming aggregate
consumers remain streaming on each alternative. Certificates describe each
presence combination; any growing alternative makes the operation grow.

Presence alternatives share a logical page site and carry a fixed-size
128-bit identity in their opaque cursor scope. Changing presence refuses
with `E_CURSOR_INDEX`, including when alternatives share an index. A search
needle folding to no terms is another absence alternative: browse using the
ordinary pins and order. Evaluate the needle once and meter its fold before
choosing. This is Quarry lowering; serialized raw words-index IR keeps its
existing behavior when no word lanes exist. Server and device interpret
the same conditional reads. Generated browse normalization touches only its
outer leaf; nested point reads and needle expressions retain their own keys.
For an explicitly selected words index, the browse leaf reuses the
lexicographically first plain index with the identical effective ordering and
computed-key definition, or synthesizes its ordinary index. This generated
choice does not relax ambiguity checks on authored predicate reads. A unique
key with any nullable component is not a total cursor order: null ties are
legal. Browse alternatives and ordinary reads with cursors reuse an index
without a declared id only when every unique component is required (including
validated calendar keys). Otherwise they synthesize or choose a separate id
ordering, preserving the unique constraint. Explicit unsafe cursors refuse
with `E_CURSOR_INDEX` and a column-ordered read rewrite. Reads without cursors
may keep their existing physical-prefix indexes; merge cursors and internal
sweep/aggregate positions already carry the physical id tiebreak. The generated
Following inbox keeps its existing unique constraints and reads through a
separate `byReaderPage` index ending in id; pending-work completeness and
live-query dependencies apply to both old and new reader indexes.

Presence-selected reads cannot supply mutation population loops or top-level
job sweeps in this implementation. Bind those as an ordinary capped loop or
stable sweep and put the optional condition in its body. Mutation admission
retains conditional scan provenance even for emit-only loops. The runtime
validates every top-level loop before running any chunk and parks stored
non-native jobs with no recorded sweep or any unsupported work loop as
`E_JOB_SWEEP`. Mixed valid/invalid sweeps cannot skip work or commit a valid
chunk first. Bounded setup loops before a recorded sweep are supported when
both their bodies and domain expressions are write-free and emit-free;
compiler-generated prefix setup, such as a list `sum`, replays under each
chunk's meter. Inner loops keep their execution. A trailing setup loop with
no following sweep is unsupported because no chunk would execute it.

A keyed `exists` in a predicate is always an ordinary authorized point
probe when it covers a total unique key. Driving from that table is only
an optimization: if its discovery prefix cannot decide its read rule,
retain the point probe per candidate and explain the skipped-row growth.
The source rule, disclosure policy, scan admission and meter are unchanged.

The index is the pins in canonical order, then any bucket key, then the order
keys, then `id`. A declared index with exactly those leading components is
used. Otherwise the compiler synthesizes one and adds it to the schema. Its
identity derives from its complete canonical descriptor: components,
computed-key parameters, words fields and uniqueness. It is independent of
declaration and program order. `check --cost` prints
every chosen and synthesized index with the read that needs it. Index
synthesis changes nothing at run time. The engine builds indexes on adoption
exactly as it does for a declared `by` line.

A predicate read that the planner can only serve as a sparse residual scan
keeps today's note (`N_SPARSE_FILTER`), with a rewrite to a pin, a view
(§3), or an order key.

### 2.2 Point reads have one meaning

`T[e]` selects identity when `e` is typed `id` or a reference to `T`, even
when other one-column unique keys exist. It means `T[id = e]` and retains
the named form's table-identity check. Otherwise the argument types must
select exactly one declared unique key of the same arity, in declared column
order. A foreign-table reference may select a unique column of that reference
type; it cannot stand in for `T`'s identity. Principals and text select compatible
unique columns. Text literals retain contextual identity conversion, so a literal
may be ambiguous between identity and text keys. Exact type equality does not
break a tie between otherwise compatible declared keys. The same selection
applies to program reads, keyed writes and rule `exists`/`created` probes.
Explicit index names retain their existing semantics. Synthesized indexes never take part in resolving a
positional key, so adding a read can never change another read's meaning. `T[col = e, …]` reads by named
columns; named equalities that cover a total (non-nullable) unique key check
any extra columns on that one row. Equalities exactly covering a declared
unique key select a point even when columns are optional, in any order.
With the same selected unique index and no residual equalities, both lower
to the same `Get`/`Exists` key in declared column order; expression setup
retains authored evaluation order. A named read prefers
the shortest covered total unique key; with `unique single: low` and
`unique pair: low, high`, it may use `single` and check `high` afterwards,
while the positional pair uses `pair`. For admitted non-null arguments these
return the same row through different plans. A competing nonunique index
does not displace an exact unique key, including in rule probes.

**Calibration #31 (0.4.13), PK ruling 2026-10-06.** The first M3 check
reported four positional-read arity refusals, two positional-rule arity refusals
and one `conversations.slug is text <=80; got id` type error. The builder
removed conversation uniqueness; the resulting slug population carried
`N_NEVER_COMPLETE`. `data_modeling` scored 87 (calibration #30: 90). The lost
first draft is not claimed as preserved: the [PK report](../snapback4/reports/20261006-pk-typed-positional-keys/REPORT.md)
distinguishes reconstructed cases from the retained log. The old arity gate
counted implicit `byId`, so `unique slug` alone produced two candidates before
argument types were considered. Type-directed point selection removes that
pressure to weaken the schema while retaining NL's named and nullable rules.

**PK round 1 (2026-10-07).** Audience index planning consumes the ordinary
rule binder's admitted key and column order before synthesizing access indexes.
It must not repeat an arity-only choice: `exists members[.conversation, viewer]`
with `unique pair: conversation, principal` and
`unique reverse: principal, conversation` binds `pair` for both the rule and
sync planning. The content prefix, inverse discovery index and any horizon
